decision_maker: Flourishing Communities Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
To provide an update on the letter sent to
local MPs in relation to Water Management and a ministerial
response
content:
The Committee considered correspondence
received in response to a letter previously sent to local Members
of Parliament regarding water management and flood response.
 
It was noted that the letter had been
circulated to a number of local MPs covering the district’s
Internal Drainage Board areas. Members were advised that only one
response had been received, from Emma Hardy MP (Parliamentary
Secretary of State) to date. The Committee expressed disappointment
at the low level of engagement, particularly given the number of
MPs contacted and the significance of the issues raised.
 
During discussion, it was highlighted that the
response received was considered to be a general political reply
and did not directly address the specific questions posed by the
Committee. Members were of the view that the response outlined
existing structures and funding arrangements but failed to engage
meaningfully with the concerns raised around local watercourse
maintenance, flood risk, and accountability.
 
The Committee discussed the role of the
Environment Agency and Internal Drainage Boards, noting concerns
that inconsistent maintenance of watercourses in some parts of the
country could increase flood risk locally. It was emphasised that
while watercourses may appear well maintained at present, a lack of
ongoing maintenance could quickly lead to blockages and associated
flooding, with potential economic and environmental
consequences.
 
Members also discussed wider national and
regional work being undertaken through sector bodies and drainage
networks, and the importance of local authorities continuing to
speak with a strong and unified voice on water management issues.
The Committee agreed that local insight and evidence must continue
to be fed into those discussions.
 
Further concern was raised regarding the lack
of clarity around decision?making processes for prioritising
watercourse maintenance, including the criteria used to assess
risk, economic impact and agricultural importance. Members
considered it important that these matters be clearly challenged
and evidenced.
 
The Committee agreed that the matter should be
pursued further and that a follow?up letter should be issued,
seeking a more direct response to the questions originally raised
and asking whether local MPs were willing to actively support the
Council’s position on water management.
 
RESOLVED:
It was agreed that:
1. 
Further correspondence be sent to Members of Parliament seeking a
substantive response to the specific questions raised in relation
to water management and flood response.
2. 
The follow?up correspondence also seek clarity on the position and
responsibilities of relevant statutory bodies, including
maintenance of watercourses.
topline: The Flourishing Communities Scrutiny Committee has decided to pursue further correspondence with Members of Parliament regarding water management and flood response.

decision_maker: Flourishing Communities Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
Update on progress against Q1 and Q2, with a
discussion around actions in advance of the next Action Plan
issue.
content:
The Committee considered the Climate Change
Action Plan, which set out the Council’s established climate
response strategy and delivery actions.
 
It was noted that the Plan contained over 50
SMART actions developed collaboratively across the organisation and
provided direction for the year ahead. Progress data showed that
during Quarter 2, 88% of actions were on track, with the remaining
actions delayed due to unforeseen circumstances and expected to be
resolved within the year. Members were advised that future
iterations of the Plan were likely to adopt a two?year format to
support longer?term planning and continuity.
 
Members welcomed the strength and clarity of
the Plan but suggested that future reviews could further strengthen
links to residents’ lived experience, including clearer
consideration of health, wellbeing and quality?of?life outcomes.
Opportunities to enhance community engagement were discussed,
particularly through parishes, ward?level initiatives and
Member?led activity.
 
The Committee highlighted the potential to
strengthen links between climate action and areas such as renewable
energy, biodiversity, transport and active travel, noting the wider
benefits for emissions reduction and public health. Members
recognised that some matters sat across statutory frameworks and
partner organisations and would require continued
collaboration.
 
Members welcomed ongoing work to support
behaviour change among residents, businesses and young people
through communications, events and community engagement, noting
that not all activity would sit directly within the Action
Plan.
 
The Committee acknowledged the challenges of
longer?term investment and delivery in the context of Local
Government Reorganisation, particularly in relation to Council
assets and infrastructure, but supported a collaborative approach
that could be carried forward into future governance
arrangements.
 
Vote:
 
Unanimous.
 
RESOLVED:
1. 
That the Climate Change Action Plan and progress made be noted.
2. 
That the points raised by the Committee be considered as part of
the next review of the Plan, including opportunities to strengthen
links to health, wellbeing, community engagement and transport.
3. 
That the move towards a two?year Action Plan be
supported to provide greater continuity and alignment with
longer?term priorities.
topline: The Flourishing Communities Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve the Climate Change Action Plan and its progress, with suggestions for future improvements.

Members also asked whether future agendas

decision_maker: Flourishing Communities Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
A review of the Corporate Enforcement
Policy
content:
The Committee considered the scheduled review
of the Corporate Enforcement Policy, previously agreed by the
Executive Board in 2023. The report set out the purpose and scope
of the Policy, and provided the proposed updated policy at appendix
1 of the report.
 
Members sought clarification on the appeals
processes referred to within the Policy. It was explained that each
relevant area of enforcement was governed by its own statutory
framework, with its own appeals process, and that the Policy sought
to provide overarching principles rather than replace those
statutory routes. It was noted that additional reference to appeals
procedures could be considered as part of the final drafting.
 
The Committee discussed the Council’s
approach to enforcement, noting that the Policy emphasised early
engagement, education and opportunities to resolve matters
informally before formal action was taken. Members asked whether
the Policy could more clearly state that proportionate but firm
action would be taken against harmful or deliberate offenders, and
whether communication of enforcement outcomes could be strengthened
to ensure transparency.
 
It was confirmed that officers already adopted
a balanced approach, taking context and cooperation into account.
It was agreed that the Policy framework could be reviewed to
reflect this in more detail. Reporting back on enforcement outcomes
would require input from multiple service areas, but officers would
explore the feasibility of including this where appropriate.
 
Members suggested that future policy reviews
would benefit from a comparison showing changes between the
existing and proposed versions, to assist scrutiny. The Committee
further discussed collaboration with neighbourhood policing teams,
noting recent and anticipated changes to policing structures. It
was advised that strong operational relationships were in place,
and that any strategic implications for future partnership working
could be considered at a future meeting.
 
Vote: Unanimous.
 
RESOLVED:

That the updated Corporate
Enforcement Policy be endorsed by the Committee.
That officers consider the
Committee’s comments regarding clarification of appeals
processes, communication of enforcement outcomes and the framing of
the Council’s enforcement approach.
That future reviews provide a
comparison between previous and proposed versions of the Policy to
support effective scrutiny.
topline: The Flourishing Communities Scrutiny Committee endorses the updated Corporate Enforcement Policy.

decision_maker: Council
purpose:
For Council to agree to commence a Community
Governance Review and approve the Terms of Reference.
content:
The Executive Board Member for Finance,
Governance and Democracy presented and proposed the report which
detailed that Bracebridge Heath Parish Council had
requested the Council undertake a Community Governance
Review.  This was in accordance with the relevant
legislation, to consider revisions to the parish boundaries of
Bracebridge Heath and Canwick to include existing and future
housing developments and support local community identity.
 
Council was asked to approve Community
Governance Review Terms of Reference, and this was duly
seconded.
 
Councillors supported the Review request and
acknowledged the observations to align the Parish boundaries
with local housing growth and identity. 
 
It was questioned whether the Review could
also take on board other land within Canwick Parish that was
expected to comprise part of the Lincoln Sustainable Urban
Extension. It was responded that the Review would look at specific
land areas now on the Bracebridge Heath boundary with existing
housing and soon to be built housing.  The Sustainable Urban
Extension would eventually reach a size to become its own parish,
and once sufficient electors were residing there, a further
Community Governance Review would be considered in
future. 
 
Vote:
 
Unanimous
 
Resolved:
 
1. 
That Council notes the request from Bracebridge Heath Parish
Council for a Community Governance Review.
 
2. 
That Council approves to undertake a Community Governance Review
covering the parishes of Bracebridge Heath and Canwick with a view
to establishing whether alteration of parish boundaries is
considered to be appropriate.
 
3. 
That Council approves the Community Governance Review Terms of
Reference.
 
4. 
That Council notes further reports will be brought to Council in
order that decisions may be made on draft proposals and final
recommendations of the Review.
topline: The Council has decided to approve a Community Governance Review for Bracebridge Heath and Canwick to consider revisions to parish boundaries.

content:
Application No. and Type:


23/0325/NSIP - Nationally Significant
Infrastructure Project – Local Impact Report (LIR).




Proposal:


Application by Fosse Green Energy Limited for
a Development Consent Order for the installation of solar (PV)
generating panels and on-site Battery Energy Storage System (BESS)
and associated infrastructure with electrical generation capacity
of 342 to 385 megawatts (MW) with storage capacity anticipated at
480 megawatt hours along with grid connection and associated
infrastructure




Location:


Fosse Green Energy Solar Park – 9km
south-west of Lincoln near Thorpe On The Hill, Morton, Witham St
Hughs, Haddington, Thurlby, Norton Disney, Bassingham and Boothby
Graffoe.




Applicant:


Fosse Green Energy Ltd - a partnership between
Windel Energy Ltd and Recurrent Energy.




Agent:


AECOM Ltd.




Reason
for Committee Consideration:


Officer referral as the proposed Nationally
Significant Infrastructure Project raises significant environmental
impacts in terms of national and local planning policy.




 
Councillor Pennell
stated for openness and transparency purposes that he had attended
Coleby and Harmston Parish Council meetings, where this item had
been discussed, but that he had not expressed an opinion. He also
stated that he had received communication this afternoon about the
application and that this had also been sent to Members of the
Planning Committee. 
 
Councillor
Carrington stated for openness and transparency purposes that he
had attended Coleby and Harmston Parish Council meetings, where
this item had been discussed, but that he had not expressed an
opinion. He also stated that he had received an email this
afternoon about the application but that he had not read it. He was
also a Member of Lincolnshire County Council but he had had no
involvement in the application or the County response.
 
Councillor Smith
stated for openness and transparency purposes that he had received
two emails this afternoon about the application.
 
Councillor Mrs
Green stated for openness and transparency purposes that she had
attended Parish Council meetings and the Fosse Green local group
but that she had an open mind to consider the application.
 
Councillor Cawrey
stated for openness and transparency purposes that she had not been
able to access the email. She was also a Member of Lincolnshire
County Council but had had no involvement in the application and
had an open mind to consider it. 
 
Councillor Wright
stated that he had received emails from Councillor Mrs Overton
about the application.
 
The Development Manager presented the
application using maps, plans and photographs to demonstrate the
location and character of the site, as well as the material issues
identified in the agenda report. He also drew Members’
attention to the relevant national and local planning policies.
 
The proposal was for a Development Consent
Order (DCO) for the installation of solar (PV) generating panels,
on-site Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) and associated
infrastructure, with electrical generation capacity of 342 to 385
megawatts (MW) and storage capacity anticipated at 480 megawatt
hours along with grid connection and associated infrastructure.
 
As this application was a Nationally
Significant Infrastructure Project (NSIP), it would be administered
by the Planning Inspectorate who would make a recommendation to the
Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, who was
responsible for determining the application under the Planning Act
2008.
 
The role of the District Council at this point
in the examination process was the submission of the Local Impact
Assessment (LIR), which the Planning Act 2008, Section 60(3),
defined as a ‘report in writing giving details of the likely
impact of the proposed development on the Authority’s area
(or any part of that area). The LIR framed the Council’s
position on the positive, neutral and negative effects of the
proposed scheme following the pre-application process, professional
review of the scheme and the accompanying
documentation.  The examination process
was currently at Stage three of six (the pre-examination
stage).
 
The Development Manager advised the Committee
that after the agenda had been published, the Planning Inspectorate
had published its draft examination timetable, and the key dates
and deadlines were:
· 
Preliminary meeting on Tuesday 6th January 2026
(AM).
· 
First Issue Specific Hearing (Environmental matters) on Tuesday
6th January 2026 (PM).
· 
A Compulsory Acquisition Hearing on Wednesday 7th
January 2026
· 
Second Issue Specific Hearing (Environmental matters) on
8th January 2026.
 
There were seven examination deadlines and the
Council’s LIR and the follow-up written representation was
due by deadline one (20th January 2026). The whole
examination process was scheduled to finish on 15th June
2026.
The seven key topic areas of most concern as
set out in the LIR (and with an associated recommendation that
Officers formally object on those grounds through their Written
Representation) were:
 
· 
Impacts on Best and Most Versatile (BMV) agricultural land.
· 
Landscape and Visual impact including residential visual
amenity.
· 
Cultural Heritage impacts (above and below ground).
· 
Ecology, Biodiversity and Biodiversity Net Gain (specifically
BNG).
· 
Rights of Way/Recreation.
· 
Grid Connection Deliverability.
· 
Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) and Fire Safety.
 
The Officer assessment was contained within
the agenda, and the recommendation was for Authority to Deal to be
granted and for Officers under delegated powers to update as
necessary and submit the LIR and subsequent Written Representation
(WR) to the Examining Authority and thereafter to engage with
further stages and deadlines of the examination process; all also
delegated to Officers. This was in relation to the Fosse Green
Solar Farm noting specific impacts and with particular focus, and
raising objections, in relation to the seven key topic areas.
 
In line with the Council’s Constitution,
the public speaking scheme was not applicable on applications such
as this one where the District Authority was a consultee and not a
decision maker. However, the relevant Local Ward Members were able
to speak on the application.
 
The meeting adjourned to allow the registered
Local Ward Members/Strong Community Advocates to address the
meeting.
 
Councillor Mrs Overton spoke as the Ward
Member for Navenby and Brant Broughton and she raised the following
points:
· 
She had circulated information to the Committee and thanked any
Member who had read it within the timescales leading up to the
meeting.
· 
The LIR was a comprehensive report reflecting many of the local
issues, however as a draft document it could be changed and
improved by Members.
· 
She felt that there was strong local feeling against these types of
applications and that was reflected in the number of letters being
sent to the Prime Minister.
· 
In general, she was supportive of the Net Zero and Renewable Energy
Policies and ‘appropriate’ schemes.
· 
The inclusion in the LIR that the Council ‘supports’
the application in principle undermined the objections raised and
it should be amended to ‘the Council supports appropriate
renewable energy’.
 
Councillor Mrs Overton had also submitted a
presentation, which was displayed on the screen and included these
topic headings:
· 
Wrong location.
· 
Site selection limited to 15km radius.
· 
Use of good farmland/impacts on Best and Most Versatile (BMV)
land.
 
Councillor Peter Overton then spoke as the
Ward Member for Witham St Hughs and Swinderby and he highlighted
the following matters:
· 
There had been a motion at Council in January 2024 against large
scale Solar developments.
· 
He acknowledged the Government’s position in supporting large
scale Solar developments but felt that it was important for Members
to look at it from a different angle and ensure that objections
were voiced.
· 
The proposal was not in the right location and other sites should
have been considered.
· 
NSIPs equated to ten per cent of the Council’s area and
Members should use their influence to block these developments.
· 
The Planning Committee should be mindful of the scale of strong
feelings against the application. 
· 
He did not agree with the inclusion in the LIR of the Council
supporting the application ‘in principle’ and felt that
it should be changed and should not be supported.
 
Councillor Mrs Overton and Councillor Peter
Overton both answered questions from a Member of the Committee and
the meeting then resumed formal session.
 
Members thanked Officers and the team for the
comprehensive report on a complex and challenging area of Planning.
The Committee debated the application in detail, considering the
Officer’s report, presentation and statements from the Local
Ward Members/Strong Community Advocates.
 
Members discussed and raised the following
considerations:
· 
It was important to note and acknowledge that applications
resulting in the loss of BMV land did not quantify the potential
impacts that such losses had on the UK’s food productivity
capabilities. There was a balance between carbon
reduction and the impacts on food production. In
Lincolnshire, agriculture represented 21% of employment and 24% of
the economy.
· 
Members had previously requested that Solar PV applications were
subject to a sequential test and queried how this was demonstrated
within the LIR.
· 
There were other sustainable alternatives available rather than
using agricultural land.
· 
Concerns about the inclusion in the LIR of the
Council ‘supporting in principle’ this
development.
· 
Impacts on landscape and visual harm and the scale
and size of the proposal in this particular location.
· 
The Council’s role in terms of submitting the
LIR conveying the positive, neutral and negative impacts, as
well as any other information to be shared with the Planning
Inspectorate. 
· 
The use of the safest rather than the most efficient
battery technology for the BESS to reduce the risks of any
incidents.
· 
There had not yet been a planning application
submitted for the proposed Navenby Substation, which was intended
to be the point of connection. 
· 
Some concern about electromagnetic fields/exposure limits (EMF)
from BESS and associated ecological impacts specifically on
bees.
· 
A financial bond/security was required to mitigate
the risk and cost of early decommissioning falling to the District
Council in the event of a cessation of energy production or the
applicant/operator going out of business.
· 
Concern about the impacts, intensity and effects on
the economy and the land from potentially sixty years of use
through this development. The unknown factors and long-term effects
of losing the agricultural land for the solar development and the
outcome after sixty years; Members were concerned that there was no
certainty that the land would have retained BMV land quality at the
point of decommissioning. 
· 
Acknowledgement that a high percentage of solar
panels could be recycled and that some of the BMV land being lost
was not currently being used for human food production purposes but
there was the potential for it to be used by the food sector. The
lack of evidence for or against the impacts of the solar
development on the land.
· 
Whether a BESS was compatible with areas of flood
risk.
· 
There was little opportunity for the Planning
Committee to explore the wide scale cumulative impacts in the
District and the County of this application, whereas the Planning
Inspectorate was able to take this on board.
· 
There was clear harm associated with the negative
impacts detailed in the LIR. The Central Lincolnshire Local Plan
(CLLP) stated that in principle renewable energy schemes would be
supported in the ‘appropriate location’. However, it
was not possible to give support for this proposal, as it had not
been determined that it was appropriately located, nor had the
negative impacts been addressed yet by the Applicant and that
appropriate mitigation or compensation for those impacts could be
secured.  Therefore, Members noted that
it was premature and without basis at the present time to
‘support in principle’ the proposals (including that
they were ‘appropriately located’) in particular in
light of the seven key points of objection proposed to be raised in
the Council’s Written Representation. On that basis Members
opined that the scheme did not align with the general
‘presumption in favour of development’ principles
contained within CLLP policy S14 ‘Renewable
Energy’.
 
In response to questions from the Committee,
the Development Manager advised that:
· 
The LIR was not a mandatory document, and the District Council had
chosen to submit the report which was a statement of positive,
neutral and negative impacts, as well as any other information that
was relevant and the District Council wished to highlight to the
Planning Inspectorate. The report would form part of the
decision-making process by the Planning Inspectorate and that once
submitted PINS and the Secretary of State had to have regard to it
in their recommendation and decision.
· 
Nationally there had been two examples through decommissioning
documents where the Applicant had either made a commitment or set
aside monies for a bond to be paid when a site was to be
decommissioned early. The need for a similar bond was included
within the LIR report. 
· 
As raised during the Member debate, there was more opportunity to
consider cumulative impacts on NSIP applications due to the
Environmental Impact Assessment Regulations’ requirement for
cumulative impacts to be addressed; and which the Applicant had
done and where the Council had provided input at the
pre-application stage.
· 
The conclusion in paragraph 29.5 of the LIR did state that the
Council therefore supports the principle but there were a number of
tensions with Policy, including the CLLP and the three
Neighbourhood Plans, which was included in the LIR. 
· 
There were also a number of Council Policies, Strategies and Plans
that aligned and supported the principles of transitioning to a
zero-carbon future and carbon reduction by 2030.
· 
As discussed by Members S14 of the CLLP did support
‘appropriately located development’ however within S14
there was also support for all principles of renewable energy and a
presumption in favour of solar developments, including the use of
BMV land. The word ‘support’ used within the LIR
conclusion could be seen as premature at this stage and could be
removed due to the seven areas of objection. The approach could
then be to see how the seven areas of objection progress through
the examination stages and where these matters would be delegated
to Officers in line with the recommendation.
· 
Most solar developments had a forty-year lifespan, and the
Applicant would need to justify a higher timescale and provide
mitigation measures as the negative effects and harm identified
would be present for a longer period (60 years). This would form
part of the examination process and was a requirement of the
National Policy Statements for energy. The site would however be
considered ‘temporary’ and reversable by the Planning
Inspectorate, and it would be decommissioned after its
lifespan.
· 
Biodiversity Net Gain was not currently mandatory for NSIP
applications and so when offered voluntarily by an Applicant it
gained planning weight. The Applicant for this development was
looking to exceed the usual 10% figure applied to other
developments.
· 
The Officer advised in relation to electromagnetic fields/exposure
limits (EMF) from the BESS and associated ecological impacts
specifically on bees that he was not aware of UK ecological
publications or guidance specifically in relation to impacts on
bees, and that the LIR should not introduce matters that could not
obviously be supported by associated guidance. The Officer advised
that he would address this matter with Cllr Elliott separately.
Furthermore, it was confirmed that citing concerns on EMF impacts
as akin to those associated with phone/telecommunications masts
could not be pursued as masts were subject to specific regulation
via the International Commission of Non-Ionizing Radiation
Protection (ICNIRP) protocol. 
 
It was therefore proposed and seconded that
Authority to Deal be granted in line with the Officer
recommendation, but with an amendment to paragraph 29.5/the overall
LIR conclusion to reflect that the Council could not support the
principle of the development nor confirm the presumption in favour
of development with reference to the strategic renewable energy
policy CLLP S14. This was due to the objections lodged and
therefore that the direct, indirect, individual and cumulative
impacts of development had not yet been proven to be
acceptable.
 
Officers would also undertake background
research on electromagnetic fields/exposure limits from BESS and
associated ecological impacts specifically on bees but this was not
for inclusion in the LIR.
 
Vote:
 
Unanimous
 
RESOLVED:
 
That Authority to Deal be granted to Officers
for authority under delegated powers to;
 
A. Update and thereafter submit the final
version of the North Kesteven LIR for Fosse Green energy solar
farm, incorporating any minor changes as necessary, to the
Examining Authority in accordance with examination deadline/s.
 
Paragraph 29.5/overall LIR conclusion to be
modified to reflect that the Council cannot support the principle
of the development nor confirm the presumption in favour of
development with reference to the strategic renewable energy policy
CLLP S14 given that there are objections lodged and therefore that
the direct, indirect, individual and cumulative impacts of
development have not yet been proven to be acceptable.
 
(Officers to also undertake background research
on electromagnetic fields/exposure limits from BESS and associated
ecological impacts specifically on bees – nb not
for inclusion in the LIR)
 
B. Submit ‘written
representations’ to the Examining Authority by the specified
deadline addressing the specific impacts set out under the chapter
headings in the LIR, with particular focus, and raising objections,
in relation to:
 
· 
Impacts on Best and Most Versatile (BMV) agricultural land.
· 
Landscape and Visual Impact including Residential Visual
Amenity.
· 
Cultural Heritage impacts (above and below ground).
· 
Ecology, Biodiversity and Biodiversity Net Gain (specifically
BNG).
· 
Rights of Way/Recreation.
· 
Grid Connection Deliverability.
· 
Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) and Fire Safety
 
C. Prepare and submit further responses,
information, documents, reports and statements as requested by the
Examining Authority into the procedural deadlines to be confirmed
by the Rule 6/Rule 8 letter.

Considerations
 
The Alcohol and Entertainment Licensing Sub
Committee in making its decision considered the application in line
with the need to promote the Licensing Objectives of Public
Nuisance, the Licensing Act 2003, Statutory Guidance issues under
Section 182 of the Act and North Kesteven District Council’s
Licensing Policy Statement, along with the relevant representation,
and the information supplied by the Applicants and the Objector at
the meeting.  
 
Decision
 
The Sub Committee did not consider there were
any conditions they could include on the licence that would address
the Objector’s concerns in relation to public nuisance.
 
The Sub Committee were content that the
application as made would promote the licensing objectives and
accordingly the Sub Committee have decided to grant the licence as

decision_maker: Alcohol and Entertainment Licensing Sub Committee
content:
The Licensing Team Leader presented the report
to consider an application under Section 18(3)(a) of the Licensing
Act 2003, for a new Premises Licence. The application had been
submitted in respect of Yaa Man Bar & Grill, 9 Market Place,
Sleaford, NG34 7SH to support the provision of the following
licensable activities:
 
Regulated Entertainment
Live Music (indoors
and outdoors)
Monday to Sunday 1100 – 0030
New Years Eve until 0130
Recorded Music
(indoors and outdoors)
Monday to Sunday 1100 – 0030
New Years Eve until 0130
Late Night
Refreshment (indoors)
Monday to Sunday 2300 – 0000
Sale of Alcohol (for
consumption on the Premises)
Monday to Sunday 1100 – midnight
New Years Eve until 0130
 
One relevant representation about the effect
of granting the Licence on the licensing objectives, had been
received from local resident Mrs Francesca Charlton. This was
regarding the potential for noise nuisance from Regulated
Entertainment provided at the premises, but specifically outside,
impacting on nearby residential premises. There were no
representations received from the Responsible Authorities.
 
The Chairman thanked the Licensing Team Leader
for the report.
 
Following questions from Members, the
Licensing Team Leader confirmed that:
· 
Since 2013 there had been low level compliance issues, at various
points and with various licence holders which had been
rectified.
· 
All the Responsible Authorities had been consulted on the
application, and no formal submissions had been received from
them.
· 
The Applicant has been in contact separately with the Licensing
Team at Lincolnshire Police.
 
The Interested Party, Mrs Charlton, addressed
the Sub-Committee and stated that in addition to herself, two other
local residents had also contacted the
Council’s Licensing Team about this application. The Chairman
advised that these could not be taken into
account and the Legal Advisor further explained that as part
of the rules of natural justice, only submitted formal
representations could be considered at the meeting, as it was not
possible to defend objections without the details. It was agreed
that these contacts would be noted but the Sub-Committee would not
include them as part of their determination of the
application. 
 
The Chairman then invited Mrs Toni
Campbell-Brown to speak as the Applicant and to present her case.
Mrs Campbell-Brown advised the Sub-Committee that:

She was the owner of the Yaa Man Bar
& Grill and had experience of working at other premises within
Sleaford.
The application would enable the Yaa
Man Bar & Grill to provide Jamaican cuisine and sell alcoholic
drinks for the same times granted to the business that previously
operated there. 
The ambience of the premises was
important for customer dining experiences and the music would be
kept at a moderate level. The Bar & Grill would open initially
from Wednesdays to Fridays (4.30pm to 9.30pm) for dinner service
and then also at the weekends.
The music at the premises would
mainly be recorded but live music had been included so the option
was there if needed and it may be used occasionally inside and
outside while customers were dining.
It was intended to use the premises
as a continuation of its previous use as a restaurant. The Bar
& Grill had opened at the weekend using a Temporary Event
Notice and there had been no reported issues.
Mrs Campbell-Brown had contacted the
Licensing Team at Lincolnshire Police for advice on the
premises.
The main aim of the licence was to
be able to serve customers and create an ambience – it was
not intended to operate like a nightclub.

 
In response to questions from Members of the
Sub-Committee, Mrs Campbell-Brown clarified that:

The outside area contained one table
which seated ten people either side and there was no intention to
seat customers outside at the moment due
to the weather.
Windows at the premises could be
closed and customers would be advised about noise levels to prevent
any potential noise disturbance. Mrs Campbell-Brown would be at the
premises most of the time and would monitor the noise levels.
Mr and Mrs Campbell-Brown were both
trained to use the CCTV system which showed images only and this
would be extended to bar staff once they were employed. Advice had
also been sought from Lincolnshire Police on this area, and the
necessary logs would be kept. 
The bar area was very small and
there was no seating.

 
In answer to questions from Mrs Charlton, Mrs
Campbell-Brown stated that:

All the entrances, exits and the
alleyway to the premises were covered by the CCTV system.
There would be moderate music during
dining service that would be monitored.

 
When asked about any noise disturbance from
the premises at the weekend, Mrs Charlton was unable to comment as
she had not been at home.
 
During the discussion and points raised by Mrs
Charlton about noise monitoring, the Licensing Team Leader informed
the meeting that there were no set decibel levels included within
Premises Licences, and if it was granted there were conditions in
place to promote the prevention of public nuisance. There should be
notices at all exits about noise and regular assessments of the
noise levels carried out by the business to ensure local residents were not disturbed.  Compliance visits were also carried out by
Officers from the Council’s Licensing Team and noise levels
should be monitored by the premises.
 
The Chairman was mindful that noise levels
could be a challenging area and somewhat subjective but that issues
with noise levels could be reported to the Council’s
Environmental Health Team. The Legal Advisor suggested that a noise
limiter could set and regulate noise levels, however there had not
been any representations received from the Environmental Health
Team about noise at the premises. But it would not be unreasonable
to add this as a condition to the Licence.
 
The Chairman invited the Interested Party to
address the Sub-Committee and Mrs Charlton explained that:

She had submitted a representation
and could already hear noise from other premises in Sleaford.
Her objection was not against the
application itself but against the times that music could be played
until every night.
She was concerned about the lack of
formal monitoring and the reliance on self-monitoring of sound
levels by the premises on whether she would be impacted or
not.
She felt that a precedent would be
set in Sleaford if this application was granted and that it was
unreasonable for the premises to be able to play music outside
until 12.30am when there were residential properties nearby.

 
In response to matters raised by Mrs
Charlton:

The Licensing Team Leader confirmed
that there were currently at least three premises in Sleaford
licensed for indoor and outdoor music after midnight and the times
applied for were not uncommon.
The Chairman acknowledged that the
premises did not have to make full use of the times applied for and
this was agreed by Mrs Campbell-Brown, who further explained that
the times covered all eventualities and meant she did not have to
re-apply each time.
The Sub-Committee Members were aware
that they could only consider information relating to the Yaa Man
Bar & Grill and not any issues experienced by Mrs Charlton with
other premises.
Mrs Charlton advised that she had
not made any complaints about the noise from other premises, as it
was occasional and she did not know who to raise this with, whereas
she expected the music from the Yaa Man Bar & Grill to be
constant. 
The Licensing Team Leader did advise
Mrs Charlton to contact the Council’s Licensing Team in
future about any issues, and they would then liaise with the
Environmental Health Team. The Chairman said that this option was
also available to all residents.

 
The Chairman invited all parties to summarise
their position.
 
Mrs Campbell-Brown wanted the Licence so the
business could operate as a restaurant for diners to enjoy food,
drinks and the ambience and she would work with the Licensing Team
to follow the necessary requirements. There was no intention to
cause any type of nuisance to the public or neighbours and she
would comply with all advice given by Lincolnshire Police. She gave
assurances that she would monitor the noise levels, carry out the
necessary checks and ask customers to leave the premises
quietly.
 
Mrs Charlton had no objection to the bar or
restaurant areas and was only concerned about the times and the
noise levels from outdoor music, as well as the self-monitoring of
the levels. 
 
All parties confirmed that they were happy
that they had said everything that they wished to.
topline: The Alcohol and Entertainment Licensing Sub Committee has decided to approve recommendations for a new Premises Licence for Yaa Man Bar & Grill, despite concerns raised by a local resident about potential noise nuisance.

content:
The Leader proposed the report which sought
Council approval to begin a statutory 28-day consultation, from 1
to 29 December 2025, on proposed private hire and hackney carriage
licensing fees for 2026/27.
 
Following objections to the 2025/26 fees, the
licensing team conducted a comprehensive review, including overhead
apportionment, resulting in reduced fees for most licences. The
revised fees, complied with Government guidance and legislation,
and were based on a cost-recovery model to ensure only
administrative costs are recouped, with any surplus or deficit
adjusted in future years.
 
Feedback from licence holders during the
consultation will inform the final Fees and Charges report,
scheduled for consideration by the Executive Board on 15 January
2026 and Full Council on 22 January 2026.

That approval be given to undertake a
consultation process on the proposed draft licensing fees for
2026/27.

2. 
Establish an independent cross-party task force to oversee the

3. 
Publish a detailed timeline for achieving full compliance with the

4.

decision_maker: Council
purpose:
To provide an update on the Local Government
Reorganisation Submission
content:
The Government’s devolution plans aimed
to reorganise local government within two-tier areas. Councils were
invited to submit initial proposals in March 2025, with final
submissions due by 28 November 2025. 
The decision to submit Local Government Reorganisation proposals to
the Secretary of State was an executive function.  However, given the significance of the matter,
views of Council would inform the Executive Board’s
consideration at its meeting scheduled for 27 November 2025.
 
The Leader presented the report which asked
Council to consider detailed proposals for reorganising Greater
Lincolnshire into two new Unitary Authorities within the
Lincolnshire County area:
 

Unitary Authority 1 being comprised
of the geographies of North Kesteven, South Kesteven and South
Holland.

 

Unitary Authority 2 being comprised
of the geographies of East Lindsey, West Lindsey, City of Lincoln
and Boston.

 
Existing unitary authorities could not be
compelled to change, so North Lincolnshire and North East
Lincolnshire Councils were not included in the proposal.
 
The Leader commended the proposals as well
thought through and compliant with the six criteria set by
Government.  He expressed thanks to
officers at North Kesteven and South Kesteven District Councils for
their detailed work, assessments, modelling and analysis in
developing the proposals.  External
specialist support was obtained for service areas not delivered by
district councils, with assumptions and risks clearly set out in
the submission. Financial figures were validated by the Finance
Team, and a joint budget was prepared to support the business
case.
 
The Council’s initial proposals had
included Rutland. Whilst this remained and option, it fell outside
the Government’s invitation area for Greater Lincolnshire and
could have rendered the bid non-compliant, risking rejection.
However, the exclusion of Rutland did not weaken the bid.
 
It was noted that the Government had recently
announced the abolition of Police and Crime Commissioners, with
responsibilities transferring to Regional Mayors/Combined
Authorities, or in their absence, council leaders. This adjustment
would be reflected in the proposal to the Executive Board.
 
In response to questions regarding South
Holland and the Council having their own proposals, the Leader
confirmed that South Holland fell within the invitation area and
could be included in our proposal and did not require their
specific agreement.
 
Members discussed democratic representation
and emphasised the importance of maintaining strong connections
between residents and councillors. Smaller unitary councils with
clear local identity, as put forward by this proposal, could
support this. There was some recognition that for residents, local
government reorganisation should simplify their contact with local
authorities.
 
While many expressed a preference to avoid
reorganisation, given the circumstances, the proposal was
considered the most balanced option. It highlighted demographic
similarities across the three districts, a shared market town focus
and combining strong economies. The unitary authority between NKDC,
SKDC, and SHDC could offer a financially stable and future-proof
option.
 
Concerns were raised about central government
political decisions potentially overriding local approaches, as
well as the significant burden of change and risks to democratic
accountability.
 
Cultural differences between councils and
staff uncertainty were acknowledged, with reassurance that regular
staff briefings would remain central to the process. Change would
be challenging alongside the continued delivery of services but
would be managed professionally, with leadership and data-driven
decisions guiding the process.
 
One Councillor raised concern regarding the
separation of North Hykeham from the City of Lincoln. Noting that
many neighbouring services were shared with the City and on this
basis they could not support the proposal.
 
It was noted that it would be for Government
to undertake its own public consultation with residents to give
them a say on specific LGR proposals, as it had done with the
priority council areas such as Surrey and now for areas like Essex
and Hampshire as part of having a Shadow Unitary Authority in place
by May 2027.
 
Members thanked officers for the considerable
amount of work to produce this clear and workable
solution.  Overall, consensus was that
the proposal was well thought out and in the best interests of
North Kesteven. 
 
Vote: 32 In Favour, 1 Against, 0
Abstentions
 
RECOMMENDED TO
EXECUTIVE BOARD:
 
That Council endorsed the proposal detailed in
appendix 1 to the report for Local Government Reorganisation in
Greater Lincolnshire to the Executive Board, creating two new
Unitary Authorities in the Lincolnshire County area: Unitary
Authority 1 being comprised of the geographies of North Kesteven,
South Kesteven and South Holland. Unitary Authority 2 being
comprised of the geographies of East Lindsey, West Lindsey, City of
Lincoln and Boston.
topline: The Council has decided to reorganise local government in Greater Lincolnshire into two new Unitary Authorities, despite concerns about central government influence and risks to democratic accountability.

Indicators had been revised for future monitoring purposes.
Consideration was given to risks associated with the current
economic climate and whether the Treasury Management Strategy

This was seconded by Councillor
Carrington.

1.

Indicators be approved.
 
2. 
That the change proposed to NKDC’s Accounting Policy be noted
to allow the capitalisation of borrowing as laid out in section
3.2.
 
3. 
To approve the increase in Operational Boundary from £128.54m
to £131.821m in line with the period 6 Capital Programme
reporting.

content:
Police and Crime
Commissioner (PCC) Update:
 
As part of this agenda item, the Chairman
provided Members with an update on PCC attending a future Committee
meeting.
 
It was noted that the PCC was held to account
by the Police and Crime Panel and not by District Councils or the
County Council.  However, the PCC did
usually offer to attend each of the District Councils once a year
to present the work being undertaken to deliver the Police and
Crime Plan, to ask Districts for their support on certain matters,
and to provide an opportunity for them to raise any issues/concerns
with him. 
 
In a non-election year, these have tended to
run in late Autumn/early Winter, after the annual survey results
were available.  This did not take place
this year as they were awaiting the settlement to be better placed
to update on what future operational delivery looks like, and this
was expected to be put in place post-Christmas.
 
The PCC does however provide quarterly reports
to the Panel summarising the work undertaken by him and the office
to deliver the Plan, which were available on the LCC website should
Members wish to access them.
 
Minutes:
 
The minutes of the meeting held on Wednesday
17th September 2025 were approved as a correct record.

location and character of the site, as well as the material issues
identified in the agenda report. He also drew Members’
attention to the relevant national and local planning policies,
including Neighbourhood Plan policies and
also the location of the site within the Conservation Area
and in relatively close proximity to
a number of listed buildings. The
Officer noted though that the case officer assessment found there
to be no impacts on heritage assets.
 
The key issues in the determination of the
application are as follows:
 
1. 
Design of the proposed extension, including within its historic
context and,
2. 
Impacts of the proposal on residential amenity.
 
There were no public speakers registered to
speak, therefore the Committee went
straight to the debate.
 
Members considered the application to be
straightforward, noting the absence of objections from statutory
bodies and no adverse impact on neighbouring properties.
 
It was proposed and seconded that the
application be granted permission in line with the Officer
recommendation and subject to the conditions detailed within the
Officer report.
 
Vote:
 
Unanimous.
 
RESOLVED:
 
That in line with the Officer recommendation,
planning permission be granted subject to the planning conditions
listed below:
 
1. 
The development must be begun not later than the expiration of
three (3) years beginning with the date of this permission.
Reason: To comply with the
provisions of Section 91 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990
as amended by Section 51 of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase
Act 2004.
 
2. 
The development hereby permitted shall be constructed entirely of
the materials details which are shown on drawing 23/CAS/04 REV B;
or in accordance with such alternatives as may be agreed in writing
with the District Planning Authority.
 
Reason: To ensure a satisfactory
external appearance in the interests of visual amenity to accord
with policy S53 of the Central Lincolnshire Local Plan (Adopted
2023) and policy 3 of the Dunston Neighbourhood Plan.
 
3. 
The development hereby permitted shall not be carried out except in
complete accordance with the details shown on the approved plans,
listed below on this decision notice.
 
Reason: To ensure that the development
takes place in accordance with the approved details.
topline: The council has decided to grant planning permission for a single storey rear extension in Lincoln.

content:
The Local Plans Manager provided a
presentation on the proposals to review the Central Lincolnshire
Local Plan adopted in 2023.
 
The presentation included information on the
following areas:
· 
The rationale behind reviewing the Local Plan now and the national
changes (the new process for plan-making, the removal of
Supplementary Planning documents as a tool, housing requirements
and transitional arrangements).
· 
Changes and the current Local Plan (housing numbers, impacts on
Policies and the end of Supplementary Planning documents).
· 
Local Government Reorganisation (changes to Local Authority
boundaries, potential challenges and the position of future
planning partners).
· 
Housing supply and the status of Local Plans across Lincolnshire
compared with the Central Lincolnshire area.
· 
Messages from Government about Local Government reorganisation and
plan-making. 
· 
The timetable for reviewing the Local Plan (a 30-month process, a
4-month advance notice period, 2 formal consultations, 3 Gateways
to pass and a 6-month examination process). 
 
During the presentation, the Committee noted
that the new style Local Plan would include more digital focus and
interactive maps, it would be shorter with fewer Policies, there
would be minimal supporting text and it would need to cover matters
previously covered by the Supplementary Planning documents. There
would be a substantial local based vision with clear objectives and
conformity with national Policies. There were also some issues to
be aware of and the formal process to review the Local Plan could
not begin until the necessary Legislation was enacted. The Local
Plans Manager did not feel it would be beneficial to be one of the
first areas to complete the new process and there was the emergence
of Spatial Development Strategy to consider.
 
Members were advised by the Local Plans
Manager that as part of the recommendation the following 10
Principles would also need to be agreed:
1. A single Local Plan to cover Central
Lincolnshire.
2. Evidence will be developed taking into
account future geographies emerging through Local Government
Reorganisation.
3. A plan to deliver sustainable growth for
the plan area.
4. A plan based on the adopted local plan,
building on its success and minimising changes where possible.
5. A short and readable plan.
6. A viable and deliverable plan.
7. A plan that will be consistent with
achieving a net zero carbon Central Lincolnshire.
8. A plan that will be consistent with
national policy and requirements.
9. Based on clear and effective engagement
that will follow a published timetable.
10.Considering work emerging on a Spatial
Development Strategy to be developed by the Mayoral Combined County
Authority, supporting that work and seeking to help inform it where
possible, to ensure alignment of strategies to deliver sustainable
development
 
The next steps would be to:
· 
Accelerate project planning and start to commission key evidence
– October 2025 – March 2026.
· 
Continue work on internal evidence gathering – Ongoing.
· 
Plan for call for sites this year – October 2025 –
December 2025.
· 
Make preparations for early engagements and passing Gateway 1
– January 2026 – July 2026.
 
In response to a question from a Committee
Member, the Local Plans Manager confirmed that:
· 
There was not currently a timetable for the Combined Authority
Spatial Development Strategy but this would be monitored and was an
area to be mindful of as part of the Local Plan review process.
Officers would continue to develop working relationships with the
Combined Authority and align the Local Plan with the necessary
Strategies as much as possible.
 
Members thanked the Local Plans Manager for
his report and were supportive of the proposed approach in
reviewing the Local Plan and the report recommendations.
 
Vote:
 
Unanimous
 
RESOLVED:
 
1. 
Approved the commencement of work on reviewing the Local
Plan. 
2. 
Agreed to a number of Principles that would guide the review of the
Local Plan.
3. 
Agreed to the publication of a preliminary, broad timetable for
this review at this early stage to be kept under review and updated
as needed by the Local Plans Manager
4. 
Agreed that a formal Local Plan review timetable would be brought
before the Committee for approval before the formal stages of the
plan-making system commenced.
topline: The council has decided to review the Central Lincolnshire Local Plan, with potential changes in housing numbers and policies.

decision_maker: Council
purpose:
To confirm the appointment of the S151
Officer/Chief Financial Officer, and consider interim arrangements
regarding the Section 151 Officer role.
content:
The Leader proposed the recommendations within
the  report as Chairman of the
Appointments and Appeals Panel, which sought acceptance and
confirmation to appoint to the position of Director of Resources
and Section 151 Officer, with effect from January 2026.  The report also included interim arrangements.
 
Following the resignation of the current
Deputy Chief Executive and Section 151 Officer, the role of
Director of Resources and Section 151 Officer was widely
advertised, and Tile Hill conducted technical assessments and
interviews to shortlist candidates.
 
The Appointments and Appeals Panel held
in-person interviews on 3 October 2025, supported by the Chief
Executive and HR team and unanimous agreed that Steven Houchin CPFA
be appointed as Director of Resources and designated section 151
Officer.
 
In addition to Mr Houchin’s professional
qualifications, he brings expertise in financial planning,
management, business analysis, and modelling, and has previously
held roles in Lincolnshire authorities.
 
To ensure continuity, the Council’s
Assistant Director of Resources, who had served as Deputy Section
151 Officer since October 2024, would be appointed as Interim
Section 151 Officer from 20 October 2025 until Mr Houchin takes up
his post.
 
This was seconded by Councillor Pennell.
 
During the debate Members welcomed the new
appointment and looked forward to working with Mr
Houchin.  Members expressed their thanks
and best wishes to the outgoing section 151 Officer.
 
Vote: Unanimous
 
RESOLVED that:-
 
1. 
The appointment of Steven Houchin, CPFA as Director of Resources
and Section 151 Officer, with effect from January 2026 be accepted
and confirmed;
 
2. 
Richard Hunt, CPFA, Assistant Director of Resources be designated
as the Council’s Section 151 Officer on an interim basis,
with effect from 20 October 2025 until such time as Steven Houchin
takes up the role.
 
3. 
The Monitoring Officer be delegated to remove the designation of
Deputy Chief Executive from the Constitution from 3 November
2025.
topline: The Council has decided to appoint Steven Houchin as the new Director of Resources and Section 151 Officer.

decision_maker: Alcohol and Entertainment Licensing Committee
purpose: Statutory Review of Licensing Policy
content:
The Chairman of the Alcohol and Entertainment
Licensing Committee, Councillor Johnston, proposed the
recommendation which sought approval of the Council’s
Licensing Policy. It was a statutory requirement to review the
Council’s Licensing Policy every 5 years as defined within
the Licensing Act 2003.
 
The current Licensing Policy Statement was due
for renewal. A public consultation was undertaken which received
two responses.
 
The consultation responses were considered in
detail alongside the Licensing Policy and the Committee were
satisfied that the suggested amendments by officers met the
requirements of legislation and the Statutory Guidance to Licensing
Authorities issued by the Home Office. 
The recommendation was duly seconded by Councillor Pennell.
 
During the debate, one Member queried whether
consultation had been far reaching given the limited
response.  They also queried whether the
policy should include environmental aspects relating to waste at
licensed premises.
 
Vote: Unanimous
 
RESOLVED that the revised Licensing Policy
Statement be adopted.
topline: The Alcohol and Entertainment Licensing Committee has decided to approve the Council's Licensing Policy after a public consultation with limited responses.

decision_maker: Executive Board
purpose:
To consider the options for potential
additional car parking provision.
content:
The Leader proposed the recommendation from
Executive Board which sought approval to drawdown £560,000 to
progress development of the old East Midlands Ambulance Service
(EMAS) site to a car park.
 
The Executive Board considered three options
for delivering better parking solutions and option two was
considered to offer the best balance of cost-effectiveness, control
and deliverability.
 
This was seconded by Councillor Pennell.
 
During the debate, Members were supportive of
the project and considered it was a good use of reserves.
 
One Member noted his lack of support for the
project and considered that there was no sensitivity to the
surrounding habitat.  He also considered
that the project should be delayed looking at alternate delivery
method.
 
In his right of reply, the Leader advised that
the site was owned by NKDC, so was able to progress with the
project at speed and the Executive Board had considered that the
project was the best use of land in line with the car parking
strategy.
 
Vote: 33 For, 4 Against and 1 Abstention
 
RESOLVED:
 
1. 
That approval be given to drawdown £560,000 from Reserves.
The requested drawdowns for approval were: £200,000 from the
“Covid Recovery” Reserve, £200,000 from the
“Our Economy” Reserve and £160,000 from General
Fund Capital Receipts. Should project costs exceed £560,000,
any additional funding would need to be drawn down from
Reserves.
 
2. 
That delegated authority be granted to the Chief Executive, in
consultation with the Leader of the Council, and the Section 151
Officer to approve any further drawdowns and to determine the
appropriate Reserves from which the funding should be sourced.
topline: The Executive Board has decided to drawdown £560,000 to develop the old East Midlands Ambulance Service site into a car park.

purpose:

Government Act 1972
content:
For openness and
transparency, both Councillors Goldson and Johnston declared an
Other Registerable Interest, as the Council had appointed them
under a statutory process to North Scarle Parish Council.
 
The Leader presented the report which outlined
the urgent action taken to temporarily appoint members to North
Scarle Parish Council.  This was a
statutory action to restore quorum and enable the Parish Council to
continue its duties.
 
The District Council’s swift response
demonstrated its commitment to supporting local governance and
ensured that North Scarle continued to receive representation and
services at a parish level.
 
The Leader expressed his thanks to the
District Councillors appointed for the additional undertaking they
had committed to assist their local parish.
 
The Leader duly proposed the recommendations
as listed in the report.  This was
seconded by Councillor Pennell.
 
Vote: Unanimous
 
RESOLVED that: -
 
1. 
The temporary appointments of District Ward Councillors, Councillor
Chris Goldson and Councillor Richard Johnston, to North Scarle
Parish Council be noted; and
 
2. 
The Monitoring Officer be authorised to make further appointments
to North Scarle Parish Council in accordance with the approved
procedure should it be necessary.
topline: The Council has decided to temporarily appoint District Ward Councillors to North Scarle Parish Council to ensure continued representation and services.

decision_maker: Audit Committee
purpose:
Annual Audit Committee Chairman's Report
2024/25
content:
The Chairman of the Audit Committee,
Councillor Mrs Hagues, proposed Council’s endorsement of the
Annual Report of the Audit Committee. 
This was seconded by Councillor Green.
 
The report provided Members with an update on
the activities undertaken by the Audit Committee during the
financial year 2024/25 as well as the core work undertaken to
support the Council’s governance arrangements and
performance.
 
In particular, for
the year 2024/2025, the Committee had met and worked on an
increasingly heavy and challenging programme of work which had a
clear focus on ensuring oversight of the Council’s financial
reporting process, internal and external audit arrangements and the
Council organisations’ systems of control.
 
The report summarised the purpose and work of
the Audit Committee during the year and provided assurance that the
Committee continued to be effective, developed its strengths and
identity and acted on any opportunity for improvement.
 
Vote: Unanimous
 
RESOLVED:
 
That the Audit Committee Chairman’s
Annual Report be approved.
topline: The Audit Committee has decided to approve the Chairman's Annual Report for the financial year 2024/25.
